newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Britain denies irradiating lobsters in Irish Sea.
newsitem.headline: Britain denies irradiating lobsters in Irish Sea.

text.p: An Irish minister voiced concern on Friday about "objectionable discharges" from a British nuclear plant after complaints that some lobsters in the Irish Sea were radioactive.

Emmet Stagg, Minister of State at the Department of Transport and Energy, said he was deeply concerned about the high levels of radioactive Technetium 99 in the Irish Sea close to Britain's Sellafield nuclear reprocessing plant.
"I will pursue these issues relentlessly with the British authorities and demand an early resolution to these objectionable discharges and other problems," Stagg said in a statement.
He said he had requested an early meeting with his British counterpart "to pursue this specific problem".
British Nuclear Fuels (BNFL) earlier dismissed allegations that discharges from the plant were turning lobsters radioactive.

Nuala Ahern, a Green Party deputy in the European parliament, had said BNFL monitoring last October showed "unprecedented danger levels" in lobsters caught off the West Cumbrian coast near the Sellafield plant.
She said concentrations of Technetium 99 had reached dangerous levels off the English coast and could spread across the Irish Sea.
BNFL said Ahern's comments were based on selective choice of its figures and said Technetium levels in November 1996 were less than one-eighth of the figure in October.
"It is the effect and not the amount of discharges which is important, and discharges at these levels have no effect whatsoever," BNFL said in a statement.
"The variation in monthly levels occurs because effluent treatment for this particular waste is done in a batch process."

The Green party is fielding more than 20 candidates in Friday's Irish elections on a platform of saving and nurturing the Irish environment, which governments say is amongst the least spoiled in Europe.
"Successive Irish governments have fudged taking action on Sellafield. This is not a political game, these discharges are lethal and have got to stop immediately," Ahern said in a statement.
Ireland has long been worried about discharges from Sellafield -- formerly known as Windscale -- and in February called in the British ambassador after two incidents within 24 hours at the complex.
A month later Dublin warned Britain it would fight plans to build an underground nuclear dump near Sellafield.
